## Last week we looked inside the person

Psychology asked what a person believes, intends, and feels, and what the
situation in front of them allows.

This week the unit of analysis changes. **Sociology asks about the patterns
that exist beyond any one person** — and that shape what any individual can
believe, intend, or do.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.2. Be explicit that this is not a
correction of psychology. It is a different level of explanation, and the two
are complementary.

**Pacing.** Full deck is 50 minutes; the core path is 42. Slides marked "If time is short, skip this slide" are the drop list: the "applied" slide and social order/social change. Protect troubles-and-issues and the pair rehearsal --- both are Friday item 1.
:::

## Today's question

When thousands of people give the same individual reason, what are we actually
looking at?

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. This is the troubles-versus-issues
question, and it is the spine of Friday's item 1.
:::

## What you should be able to do

By the end of today, you should be able to:

- distinguish **structure** and **agency**, and explain why you need both;
- define a **social fact** and distinguish a private **trouble** from a public
  **issue**;
- explain **social construction** and give a fish-and-wildlife example; and
- define **social order** and **social change**.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.1–9.3.5. Wednesday adds the three
theoretical perspectives and the core concepts of socialization, community, and
stratification.
:::

## Structure and agency {background-color="#123f5a" .section-slide}

Society shapes people. People reshape society.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1.
:::

## Two words, one relationship

::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}

**Structure**

The stable, patterned relationships among societal elements that influence
human action: institutions, roles, norms.

:::::
::::: {.column width="50%"}

**Agency**

The capacity of individuals to act independently and make choices.

:::::
:::

::: {.key-idea}
Structuration: people's interactions create and renegotiate structures, while
individuals act within the contexts those structures produce.
:::

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1. Giddens' point is mutual
dependence, not a compromise between two positions. Do not let students
translate it as "some of each."
:::

## The river and its banks

A river's **banks** guide its **flow**.

The flow gradually **reshapes the banks**.

::: {.key-idea}
Society influences human behavior while individuals actively reshape society.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1. This is the chapter's own analogy
and it is the fastest way to recover the concept when a group collapses into
pure structure or pure choice on Friday. Ask: what would it mean to say the
river "chose" its course? What would it mean to say the banks are the whole
story?
:::

## Applied: why did participation change?

A sociologist asks structural questions:

- Has urbanization made the landscape harder to access?
- Have rural communities — traditionally a primary source of social support for
  hunting — declined in population?
- Have those areas changed in **character**, even where headcount held?

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.1 and Box 9.1. Box 9.1 notes that
urbanization is the demographic trend most strongly associated with reducing
participation, and that most demographic trends dampen it. Note the third
bullet: character can change while population does not. Friday's Exhibit A is
built on exactly that distinction.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Social facts {background-color="#2f6b57" .section-slide}

Values, norms, and structures that exist outside any one person.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2.
:::

## Durkheim's move

The decision to die by suicide is intensely personal. Yet rates vary
enormously across places, groups, and eras.

::: {.key-idea}
An explanation that works only at the individual level cannot explain why the
**rate** differs. Durkheim found social support to be a strong predictor of
aggregate rates.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Handle this example with care and
keep it brief and analytic. The methodological point is what matters: a purely
individual explanation cannot account for variation in an aggregate rate. That
move is the foundation of the discipline.
:::

## Troubles and issues

C. Wright Mills:

::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}

**Troubles**

Private experiences. One person's schedule got busier. One person lost a place
to hunt.

:::::
::::: {.column width="50%"}

**Issues**

The same troubles, when they become widespread across a population — and point
to structural change.

:::::
:::

::: notes
Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Work the chapter's own example: a
survey shows hunters quit because of "no time" or "nowhere to go." On the
surface, individual troubles. But their broad distribution asks different
questions — has leisure time declined generally? has land conversion or
posting increased in certain regions? This is precisely Friday's item 1, and
the case brief supplies the county data that converts one into the other.
:::

## Social construction {background-color="#123f5a" .section-slide}

Concepts created through human interaction and maintained by collective
agreement.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3.
:::

## Game fish and rough fish

Both are real animals. The **categories** are social constructs.

- "Game fish" are constructed as desirable, so policy promotes them: creel,
  length, and gear limits.
- "Rough fish," often **native** species, are constructed as less valuable — so
  many go unregulated entirely: no creel, bag, or gear limit.

::: {.key-idea}
Saying a category is socially constructed does not mean it is imaginary. It
means the agreement is what produces the regulation.
:::

::: notes
Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3. This is the best example in the
chapter because the management consequence is so concrete. Also cover
"endangered": we designate a species endangered because we decided a population
has fallen below a socially acceptable threshold warranting intervention. The
threshold is a social judgment applied to a biological measurement.
:::

## What is not socially constructed

Gravity. Temperature. Thermodynamics.

::: {.key-idea}
Professionals constantly negotiate the tension between biophysical realities
that no belief can alter and social constructions that determine what we do
about them.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.3. Insert this deliberately. Students
either over-apply social construction to everything or dismiss it as relativism;
this slide forecloses both. "Wilderness," by contrast, is a construct carrying
cultural, symbolic, and political significance — the same physical place is
viewed very differently by different people and cultures.
:::

## Social order and social change

**Social order:** the structures, institutions, facts, and constructs that
maintain stability — and which can also produce inequalities of status, role,
and position.

**Social change:** transformation of basic social structures and institutions
over time, often originating in economics, politics, technology, or natural
realities.

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.3.4–9.3.5. Give the chapter's
management example of social order: traditional agency funding structures often
prioritize license buyers, positioning other publics lower in a perceived
hierarchy — which influences whose interests are included. That connects
directly back to Week 5's governance and funding discussion. For social change,
use the 1970s environmental movement: culture, politics, and natural realities
shifting at once.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Pair rehearsal: trouble or issue?

With a partner, decide which each is, and name the structural question you
would ask:

1. "I lost my hunting spot when the neighbor sold the farm."
2. 63% of lapsed hunters in a county say they have "nowhere to go."
3. "I don't have time anymore."
4. Commuting over 30 minutes rose from 19% to 46% of county residents.

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Items 1 and 3 are troubles as
stated; 2 and 4 are the same content as issues. The useful answer names the
structural question — who sold, to whom, and why did that pattern accelerate?
All four figures appear in Friday's case brief.
:::

## Wednesday and Friday

**Wednesday:** the three sociological perspectives, plus socialization,
identity, community, place, and stratification.

**Before Friday:** read the **Week 08 Case Brief: Who Still Hunts Cedar
County?** It is a separate document in the Canvas module and is required
preparation.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 9, §§9.4–9.6. Set the frame now: the county is
fictional, no claim is made about any real community, and no student will be
asked to account for their own background or family.
:::

## Close

::: {.key-idea}
When thousands of people give the same private reason, the reason has stopped
being private. That is the moment a management problem becomes a sociological
one.
:::

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 9, §9.3.2. Restate the quiz deadline and the
case-brief reading expectation.
:::
